questions.q: In this lesson's example, what are the three modules and what does each one own?
options: network, backup, and monitoring, each managing a different Azure subscription
dev, staging, and prod, each a separate module for one environment
A single module that creates all resources in one main.tf
network (a VNet and subnets), compute (a VM and network interface), and database (a SQL server and firewall rule)
questions.explain: The composition is three modules, each responsible for one layer: network, compute, and database, wired together in the root configuration.

questions.q: What does `subnet_id = module.network.subnet_ids[0]` inside the `compute` module block accomplish?
options: Has no real effect — it is only a comment-style placeholder
Creates a brand-new subnet separate from the one network created
Passes network's actual output subnet ID into compute, so it can never drift out of sync with a hand-typed value
Deletes the first subnet created by the network module
questions.explain: Referencing module.network.subnet_ids[0] wires compute directly to whatever subnet network actually created, with no value copied by hand.

questions.q: Why doesn't `module "database"` need an explicit `depends_on` to ensure `module "compute"` runs first?
options: Terraform always runs modules in alphabetical order by default
Because database's input (allowed_ip) directly references compute's output, and that reference is itself an implicit dependency Terraform detects automatically
Database modules are always applied last by convention, with no dependency tracking involved
depends_on is required for every module regardless of references
questions.explain: When one module's input references another module's output, Terraform's dependency graph already knows the referenced module must be created first — no depends_on needed.

questions.q: According to this lesson, why does each module staying 'independently testable' matter even once it's part of a larger composed environment?
options: Each module can still be called on its own with made-up input values, the same way testing one function in isolation beats running an entire script
It has no practical benefit — it's only a theoretical property
Independent testability means the modules no longer need version pins
It means the modules can never be composed together at all
questions.explain: Because network, compute, and database each do one job with their own inputs/outputs, any one of them can be tested alone, independent of the full composed environment.

questions.q: What is actually new about Terraform syntax in this lesson's composition, compared to Lesson 14's single module call?
options: A brand-new 'compose' block that did not exist in earlier lessons
A special multi-module.tf file required for any composition
The version argument becomes mandatory only when composing more than one module
Nothing new — it's the same module block and module.<name>.<output> syntax, just used three times and chained together
questions.explain: Composition reuses the exact same module block and output-reference syntax already introduced in Lesson 14 — it's just applied repeatedly and chained together.
